newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair celebrates birthday with policy blitz.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair celebrates birthday with policy blitz.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Tuesday raised interest rates and gave the Bank of England freedom to set future rates in a bold move designed to keep up political momentum after last week's landslide election victory.

Aides quoted Blair, celebrating his 44th birthday on Tuesday, as calling the move a decisive act of leadership that showed Labour was intent on hitting the ground running and redeeming its core election manifesto commitments.
"It shows we will shrink from no decision that helps the long-term prosperity of Britain and its people," the aide said after the quarter point rise in rates to 6.25 percent.
Share and bond prices soared as financial markets welcomed the surprise news. "It's incredibly bold and a welcome step," said John Shepperd, chief econonomist at Yamaichi International.

New Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, living up to his pre-election nickname of the "Iron Chancellor", said: "This is the time to take the tough decisions we need for the long-term interests and prosperity of the country.
"I will not shrink from the tough decisions needed to deliver stability for long-term growth."
In stark contrast, candidates to take over the Conservative Party leadership from John Major after last week's humiliating defeat squabbled over who was backing who as new names emerged.
Outgoing interior minister Michael Howard and Eurosceptic John Redwood said they would take on fellow right-winger Peter Lilley and centrist former finance minister Kenneth Clarke.

But Howard's bid to get outgoing Welsh Secretary William Hague, just 36 and already tipped as favourite, to back him collapsed. Howard confirmed media reports that he and Hague reached a pact on Monday night, sealed in a toast of champagne.
Under the accord, Howard would have stood for the leadership and, if successful, made Hague his deputy. But Hague changed his mind and is now expected to join the race on Wednesday.

Blair also made clear there will be no let-up on the ruthless discipline which took the Labour party he has dragged from the left to the political centre to its stunning victory, ending 18 years of Conservative rule.

The new prime minister is set to tell all 419 Labour members of parliament on Wednesday that their large majority -- 179 over the Conservatives -- gives them an added responsibility to govern in the same disciplined way as it ran for office.
Blair, learning from the mistakes of past Labour administrations, is keen to ensure that the parliamentary party is a source of support for, not opposition to, the government.

As part of his strategy to ensure this, Peter Mandelson, a close Blair confidante who masterminded Labour's election campaign, will chair a meeting every morning aimed at getting across the government's message as policy unfolds.
The meeting will be attended by members of Blair's private office, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott and Brown.
